Isaac prayed before the Lord for his wife because she was barren. The Lord answered him, and his wife Rebekah conceived.
Her children struggled within her womb. She said, “If this is how it is, why am I alive?” And she went to inquire of the Lord.
And the Lord said to her, “Two peoples are in your womb, and two nations will separate from your womb. One nation will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.”
And when her time to give birth was complete, there were twins in her womb.
The first came out reddish, covered all over with curls of hair, and he was named Esau.
And afterward his brother came out, his hand holding Esau’s heel, and he named him Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she gave birth to them.
The boys grew up. Esau became a skilled hunter, a man of the open country, while Jacob was an upright man who lived in a tent.
Isaac loved Esau because he ate the game he hunted, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
Jacob was cooking a stew when his brother Esau came in from the field, exhausted.
Esau said to Jacob, “Let me eat some of that red, red stew, because I am exhausted.” That is why he was named Edom.
Jacob said to him, “Sell me your birthright today.”
Esau said to himself, “Look, I am about to die. What use is the birthright to me?”
Jacob said to him, “Swear to me today.” So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.
Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew to eat. He ate and drank, got up, and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
There was a famine in the land, besides the earlier famine in Abraham’s days. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gadar.
The Lord appeared to him and said, “Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land that I tell you.
“Live in this land, and I will be with you and bless you, because I will give all these kingdoms to you and your descendants. I will fulfill the oaths I swore to Abraham your father.”
I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven, and I will give your descendants all these lands. Through your descendants all the nations of the earth will be blessed.”
Because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my requirements, my commandments, my covenants, and my laws.
Isaac settled in Gerar.
The men of the place asked him about his wife, and he said, “She is my sister.” He was afraid to say, “She is my wife,” lest the men of the place kill him because of Rebekah, for she was beautiful.
When he had been there a long time, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked out through a window and saw Isaac playing affectionately with Rebekah his wife.
Abimelech summoned Isaac and said to him, “Look, she is your wife! How could you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac said to him, “Because I thought I might die because of her.”
Abimelech said to him, “What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.”
Abimelech commanded all the people, saying, “Anyone who harms this man or his wife will certainly be put to death.”
Isaac sowed in the land and reaped a hundredfold harvest of barley that year. The Lord blessed him.
The man grew wealthy and continued to grow wealthier until he was very wealthy.
He owned flocks, herds of cattle, and a large workforce, and the Philistines envied him.
The Philistines had stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, filling them with earth.
Abimelech said to Isaac, “Go away from us, for you have become much more powerful than we are.”
Isaac left there, camped in the valley of Gerar, and settled there.

And Isaac dug again the wells of water that his father’s servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, and that the Philistines had filled in after Abraham died. He gave them the same names his father had given them.
Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh spring water there.
The herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac’s herdsmen, saying, “The water is ours.” He named the well Esek because they disputed with him.
They dug another well, and they quarreled over that one too. He named it Sitnah.
He moved away from there, and they dug another well. They did not quarrel over it, so he named it Rehoboth and said, “Now the Lord has made room for us, and we will multiply in the land.”
He went up from there to Beersheba.

The Lord appeared to him that night and said to him, “I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of Abraham my servant.”
He built an altar there and called on the name of the Lord. He pitched his tent there, and Isaac’s servants dug a well there.
Abimelech came to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his friend and Phicol, the commander of his army.
Isaac said to them, “Why have you come to me? You hated me and sent me away from you.”
They said to him, “We have clearly seen that the Lord is with you, so we said, ‘Let there be oaths between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you,
that you will do us no harm, just as we did not harm you, but treated you well and sent you away in peace.’ You are now blessed by the Lord.”
He prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
They rose early in the morning and swore an oath to one another. Isaac sent them away, and they left him in peace.
That same day Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug. They said to him, “We have found water.”
He named it Sheba. That is why the town is called Beersheba to this day.
When Esau was forty years old, he married Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hivite.
They made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac grew old and his eyes became too dim to see, he called his older son Esau and said to him, “My son.” He answered, “Here I am.”
Isaac said to him, “Look, I have grown old, and I do not know the day when I will die.
Now take your equipment, your sword and your bow, and go out into the wilderness and hunt some game.
Prepare a dish the way I like it, and bring it to me to eat, so that I may bless you before I die.”
Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his son Esau. Esau went out into the field to hunt game and bring it back.
Rebekah said to her son Jacob, “Listen, I heard your father say to your brother Esau,
‘Bring me some game and prepare a dish for me to eat, so that I may bless you before the LORD before I die.’
Now, my son, obey me in what I command you.
“Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats from there, and I will prepare them as a dish for your father, just as he likes.”
Take it in to your father so that he may eat and bless you before the LORD before his death.”
Jacob said to his mother Rebekah, “Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned.
Perhaps my father will feel me, and I will seem to him like someone mocking him. Then I will bring curses on myself rather than blessings.”
His mother said to him, “Let your curses fall on me, my son. Only obey me, and go and get them for me.”
And he went, took them, and brought them to his mother. His mother prepared a dish just as his father liked.
Rebekah took the fine clothes of her older son Esau, which she had with her in the house, and dressed her younger son Jacob in them.
She put the skins of the young goats over his hands and over the smooth part of his neck.
She gave her son Jacob the dish and the bread she had prepared.
He went in to his father and said, “My father.” He answered, “Here I am.” Then he said, “Who are you, my son?”
Jacob said to his father, “I am Esau, your firstborn son. I have done as you told me. Get up, sit down, and eat some of my game, so that your soul may bless me.”
Isaac said to his son, “How did you find it so quickly, my son?” He answered, “Because the LORD your God provided it for me.”
Isaac said to his son Jacob, “Please come closer so that I can feel you, my son, to see whether you really are my son Esau or not.”
Jacob came closer to his father Isaac, who felt him and said, “The voice is Jacob’s, but the hands feel like Esau’s.”
He did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau, and he blessed him.
He said, “Are you really my son Esau?” He answered, “I am.”
He said to him, “Bring it to me so that I may eat some of my son’s game, so that my soul may bless you.” He brought it to him, and he ate. He also brought him wine, and he drank.
His father Isaac said to him, “Come near and kiss me, my son.”
He came near and kissed him. He smelled the scent of his clothes, blessed him, and said, “See, the scent of my son is like the scent of a field that the Lord has blessed.
May God give you some of the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, and an abundance of grain and wine.
May peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be chief over your brothers, and may your mother’s sons bow down to you. Cursed are those who curse you, and blessed are those who bless you.”
When Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had left his father Isaac, his brother Esau came back from his hunt.
He too prepared a dish and brought it to his father. He said to his father, “Let my father get up and eat some of his son’s game, so that your soul may bless me.”
His father Isaac said to him, “Who are you?” He said, “I am Esau, your firstborn son.”

Isaac was overcome with very great and profound astonishment. He said, “Who, then, was the one who hunted game and brought it to me? I ate some of everything before you came, and I blessed him. Indeed, he will be blessed.”
When Esau heard his father’s words, he let out a very loud and bitter cry. He said to his father, “Bless me too, my father!”
His father said to him, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessings.”

Esau said, “He was rightly named Jacob, for he has deceived me these two times. He took my birthright, and now he has received my blessings!” Esau said to his father, “Have you not left a blessing for me?”
Isaac answered Esau, “Look, I have made him chief over you, and I have given him all his brothers as servants. I have sustained him with grain and wine. What, then, can I do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father, “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, my father!” Then Esau raised his voice and wept.
His father Isaac answered him, “Look, your dwelling will be in the richness of the earth, and with the dew of heaven from above.”
“You will live by your sword and serve your brother. But if you turn back, his yoke will be removed from your neck.”
Esau hated Jacob because of the blessings with which his father had blessed him. Esau said to himself, “Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, and I will kill my brother Jacob.”
Rebekah was told the words of her older son Esau. She sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, “Look, your brother Esau is threatening to kill you.
Now, my son, listen to me. Get up and go to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay there a few days, until your brother’s anger calms down,
until your brother’s anger toward you passes and he forgets what you did to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there. Why should I be bereaved of both of you in one day?”
Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob takes a wife from among the Hittite women, like these women of the land, what good is my life to me?”
Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, and instructed him, saying, “Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.”
“Get up and go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father. Take a wife from there, from among the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother.
May God Almighty bless you, make you fruitful, and multiply you, so that you become a community of peoples.
May he give you the blessings of Abraham, to you and to your descendants with you, and give you as your inheritance the land where you live as a foreigner, which God gave to Abraham.”
Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.

Esau saw that Isaac had blessed his brother Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that, when he blessed him, he commanded him, “Do not take a wife from among the Canaanite women.”
Jacob obeyed his father and mother and went to Paddan-aram.
Esau saw that the Canaanite women displeased his father Isaac.
So Esau went to Ishmael and took Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, and the sister of Nebaioth, as his wife in addition to the wives he already had.
Jacob left Beersheba to go to Haran.
He came to a certain place and spent the night there because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of that place, put it under his head, and lay down in that place.
He saw in his dream a ladder standing on the earth, with its top reaching heaven, and God’s angels going up and down on it.
The Lord stood above it and said, “I am the Lord, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. The land on which you are lying I will give to you and your descendants.

Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the east and west, to the north and south. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your descendants.
I am with you and will protect you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.”
Jacob woke from his sleep and said, “The Lord is truly in this place, and I did not know it!”
Jacob was very afraid and said, “How fearsome this place is today! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
Jacob got up early in the morning, took the stone he had put under his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on its top.
Jacob named that place Bethel, though the place had previously been called Luz.
Jacob made a vow, saying, “If God will be with me and protect me on this journey I am making, and give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,
“And I return safely to my father’s house, the Lord will be my God.”
then this stone that I have set up as a pillar will be God’s house, and of everything you give me I will surely give you a tenth.”
Jacob set out and went to the land of the people of the east.
He looked and saw a well in the field, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it, because the flocks drank from that well. A large stone covered the mouth of the well.
All the flocks would gather there, and they would roll the stone away from the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they would put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
Jacob said to them, “My brothers, where are you from?” They said to him, “We are from Haran.”
He said to them, “Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?” They said to him, “We know him.”
He said to them, “Is he well?” They said to him, “He is well. Look, his daughter Rachel is coming with the sheep.”
Jacob said to them, “Look, it is still broad daylight. It is not time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep and go pasture them.”
They said to him, “We cannot until all the flocks have gathered and the stone is rolled away from the mouth of the well. Then we water the sheep.”
While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess.

When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother, Jacob went over and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well and watered the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother.
Jacob kissed Rachel, raised his voice, and wept.
Jacob told Rachel that he was a relative of her father and that he was Rebekah’s son. She ran and told her father.
When Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. Jacob told Laban all these things.
Laban said to him, “You are truly my own bone and flesh.” Jacob stayed with him for a month.
Laban said to Jacob, “You are indeed my relative, but should you work for me for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be.”
Laban had two daughters. The older was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel.
Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in appearance and lovely in figure.
Jacob loved Rachel and said, “I will work for you for seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter.”
Laban said to him, “It is better for me to give her to you than to give her to another man. Stay with me.”
Jacob worked seven years for Rachel, but they seemed to him like only a few days because he loved her.
Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, because the time is up, so that I may sleep with her.”
Laban gathered all the men of the place and held a feast.
When evening came, he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her.
Laban gave his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her servant.
When morning came, Jacob saw that it was Leah. He said to Laban, “What have you done to me? Wasn’t it for Rachel that I worked for you? Why have you deceived me?”
Laban said to Jacob, “It is not done that way in our country, to give the younger daughter before the older.
Finish this woman’s wedding feast, and I will give you the other one too, in return for working with me for another seven years.”
Jacob did so and completed her wedding feast. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant.
Jacob slept with Rachel too, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. He worked with Laban for another seven years.
The Lord saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
Leah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Reuben and said, “Because God has seen my affliction, my husband will now love me.”
She conceived again and gave birth to a son. She said, “Because the Lord has heard that I am hated, he has given me this son too.” She named him Simeon.
She conceived again and gave birth to a son. She said, “This time my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons.” That is why she named him Levi.
She conceived again and gave birth to a son. She said, “This time I will praise the Lord.” That is why she named him Judah. Then she stopped having children.
Rachel saw that she was not bearing children for Jacob, and she became jealous of her sister. She said to Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die!”
Jacob became angry with Rachel and said to her, “Am I in God's place, who has withheld children from your womb?”
She said to him, “Here is my slave woman Bilhah. Sleep with her, and let her give birth on my knees, so that I too may be comforted through her.”
She gave him her slave woman Bilhah as a wife, and he slept with her.
Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel said, “God has [?], and he has also heard my voice and given me a son.” Therefore she named him Dan.
Rachel's slave woman Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob another son.
Rachel said, “I asked the Lord and pleaded alongside my sister, and I have also succeeded.” She named him Naphtali.
Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, so she took her slave woman Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Leah's slave woman Zilpah bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, “My good fortune has come!” She named him Gad.
Leah's slave woman Zilpah bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, “What praise is mine, for the women have praised me!” She named him Asher.
Reuben went out during the wheat harvest and found mandrakes in the field. He brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, “Give me some of your son's mandrakes.”

Leah said to her, “Is it not enough for you that you have taken my husband? Will you also take my son's mandrakes?” Rachel said, “Then he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes.”
Jacob came in from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him. She said, “You are to come to me, because I have indeed hired you with my son's mandrakes.” He slept with her that night.
God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, “God has given me my wages because I gave my slave woman to my husband.” She named him Issachar.
Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Leah said, “God has endowed me with a good gift. This time my husband will be attached to me, because I have borne him six sons.” She named him Zebulun.
Afterward she bore a daughter and named her Dinah.
God remembered Rachel. God heard her and opened her womb.
She conceived and bore a son and said, “God has taken away my disgrace.”
She named him Joseph and said, “May God add another son for me.”
When Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Send me away so that I may go to my own place and my own land.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, and let me go, for you know the work I have done in your service.”
Laban said to Jacob, “If I have found favor in your eyes, I have learned by experience that the Lord has blessed me because of you.”
He said, “Name the wages I owe you, and I will pay them.”
Jacob said to him, “You know how I have served you and how your livestock have fared under my care.
For you had little before I came, but it has increased greatly, and the Lord has blessed you because of me. Now what shall I do to provide for my own household as well?”
Laban said to him, “What shall I give you?” Jacob said to him, “You need not give me anything. If you will do what I tell you, I will again tend and guard your flock.

I will pass through your entire flock today and set aside for myself every spotted and speckled lamb, every black lamb among the white sheep, and every speckled and spotted goat. These will be my wages.

My honesty will testify for me, as it does today, when you come tomorrow to inspect my wages. Any goat in my possession that is not spotted or speckled, and any sheep among the white ones that is not black, will count as stolen.”
Laban said to him, “Yes, let it be as you say.”

That day he separated the spotted and speckled male goats, all the spotted and speckled female goats, all those with any white on them, and all the black sheep among the white ones. He put them in the care of his sons.
He put a three-day journey between himself and Laban, and Jacob tended the rest of Laban’s flock.
Jacob took fresh white rods from almond and plane trees. He peeled white strips in them, exposing the white wood of the rods.
He set the rods he had peeled in the water channels, at the watering place where the flocks came to drink, directly in front of the flocks. They came into heat when they came to drink.
The flocks mated in front of the rods, and the flocks gave birth to white-marked and speckled young.

Jacob separated the spotted and speckled lambs and all the black animals in Laban’s flock and placed them in front of the flock. He made a separate flock for himself and did not mix them with Laban’s flock.
Whenever the early-breeding animals came into heat, Jacob placed the rods in front of the flock in the water channels, so that they would mate by the rods.
But he did not put them there for the late-breeding animals. So the late-breeding animals belonged to Laban, and the early-breeding animals to Jacob.
The man became exceedingly wealthy. He had large flocks, male and female slaves, female donkeys, camels, and male donkeys.
Jacob heard Laban’s sons saying, “Jacob has taken everything our father had, and from what belonged to our father he has acquired all this wealth.”
Jacob saw from Laban’s expression that his attitude toward him was not what it had been before.
The Lord said to Jacob, “Return to the land of your ancestors and to your relatives, and I will be with you.”
Jacob sent for Rachel and Leah to come to the field where his flock was.
He said to them, “I see that your father’s attitude toward me is not what it was yesterday and the day before. But the God of my father has been with me.”
“You yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength.
Yet your father has deceived me and changed my wages ten times. But God has not allowed him to harm me.
If he said, ‘The spotted animals will be your wages,’ all the flock gave birth to spotted young. If he said, ‘The speckled animals will be your wages,’ all the flock gave birth to speckled young.
God has taken some of your father’s livestock away and given them to me.
When the flock was in heat, I looked up and saw in a dream that the male goats mounting the flock were spotted, speckled, and mottled.
The angel of God said to me in the dream, ‘Jacob!’ I said, ‘Here I am.’
And he said to me, “Look up and see: all the male goats mating with the flock are white-marked, spotted, and speckled, because I have seen everything Laban has done to you.”
“I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar for me and made a vow to me. Now get up, leave this land, and return to the land of your birth.”
Rachel and Leah answered, “We no longer have any share or inheritance in our father’s household.
He regards us as foreigners, since he sold us and has also used up our money.
All the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and our children. So now do everything the Lord has told you.”
Then Jacob got up and put his children and his wives on camels.
He drove away all his livestock and took all the possessions he had acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s idols.
Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was leaving.
He fled with everything he had. He set out, crossed the river, and headed toward the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day, Laban was told that Jacob had fled.
He took his relatives with him and pursued Jacob for a seven-day journey, catching up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream at night and said to him, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.”
Laban caught up with Jacob. Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban settled his relatives in the hill country of Gilead.
Laban said to Jacob, “What have you done, deceiving me and carrying off my daughters like captives taken by the sword?
Why did you flee in secret and steal away from me without telling me? I would have sent you off with joy and singing, with harps and tambourines.
You did not even let me kiss my children and my daughters. You have acted foolishly in what you have done.
I had the power to harm you, but your father’s God said to me last evening, ‘Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.’
Now, you have indeed gone because you longed so deeply for your father’s home. But why did you steal my gods?”
Jacob answered Laban, “Because I was afraid and thought you might take your daughters away from me.
Whoever is found with your gods must not live. In the presence of our relatives, identify anything of yours that I have, and take it.” Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.
Laban entered Jacob’s tent, Leah’s tent, and the tent of the two slave women, but he found nothing. He left Leah’s tent and entered Rachel’s tent.
Rachel had taken the idols, put them in the camel’s saddle, and sat on them. Laban felt through the whole tent but found nothing.
Rachel said to her father, “Do not be angry, my lord, because I cannot stand up before you, since I am having my period.” He searched but did not find the idols.
Jacob became angry and argued with Laban. Jacob said to Laban, “What is my offense? What is my sin, that you have pursued me?
You have felt through all my belongings. What have you found of all the belongings of your household? Put it here before my relatives and yours, and let them judge between the two of us.
I have been with you these twenty years. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flock.
I did not bring you any animal that had been torn apart. I watched over it, for you demanded it from my hands, whether it was stolen by day or stolen by night.
By day the heat consumed me, and by night the frost, and sleep fled from my eyes.
I have now spent twenty years in your household. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the One feared by Isaac, had not stood by me, you would now have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my hardship and the toil of my hands, and he rebuked you last night.

Laban answered Jacob, “The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, and the flock is my flock. Everything you see is mine. But what can I do today to these daughters of mine, or to the children they have borne?
Now come, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between me and you.”
Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
Jacob said to his relatives, “Gather stones.” They took stones and made a heap, and they ate there at the heap.
Laban called it the Heap of Witness, and Jacob called it Galeed.
Laban said, “This heap is a witness between me and you today.” That is why he named it Galeed.
It was also called Mizpah, because he said, “May the Lord watch between me and you when we are apart from each other.
If you mistreat my daughters, or if you take other wives besides my daughters, even though no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between me and you.”
Laban said to Jacob, “Here is this heap, and here is this pillar that I have set up between me and you.
This heap is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I will not pass beyond this heap to you, and that you will not pass beyond this heap and this pillar to do harm.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of our fathers, judge between us.” And Jacob swore by the One feared by his father Isaac.
Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat bread. They ate bread and spent the night on the mountain.
Laban rose early in the morning, kissed his sons and daughters, and blessed them. Then Laban left and returned to his own country.
Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, “This is God’s camp.” He named that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau, to the land of Seir, the territory of Edom.
He instructed them, saying, “This is what you must say to my lord Esau: ‘Your servant Jacob says: I have lived with Laban and remained there until now.
I have acquired cattle, donkeys, flocks, male servants, and female servants. I have sent word to inform my lord, so that I may find favor in your eyes.’”
The messengers returned to Jacob and said to him, “We went to your brother Esau, and he is now coming to meet you, with four hundred men.”
Jacob was afraid and deeply distressed. He divided the people with him, along with the flocks, cattle, and camels, into two camps.
Jacob said, “If my brother Esau comes against one camp and destroys it, the remaining camp will escape.”
He prayed and said, "God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, LORD, who said to me, ‘Return to the land of your fathers and to your relatives, and I will do you good.’
I am unworthy of all your kindness and all the faithfulness you have shown your servant. For I crossed this Jordan with only my staff, and now I have become two camps.
Rescue me from the hands of my brother Esau, for I am afraid of him, that he may come and strike me down, mother and children alike.
“You said, ‘I will surely do good to you and make your descendants like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because it is so plentiful.’”
He spent that night there and took from what he had with him a gift for his brother Esau:
Two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
Thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten young donkeys.
He put them in the care of his servants, each herd separately, and said to his servants, "Go ahead of me, and leave space between one herd and the next."
He instructed the first servant, saying to him, "When my brother Esau meets you and asks you, ‘Whose servant are you? Where are you going? And whose are these animals ahead of you?’
Say to him, ‘They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift he has sent to my lord Esau, and he himself is coming behind us.’"
He also instructed the second and the third, and all who were following the herds, saying, "Say these same words to Esau when you meet him.
And tell him, ‘Your servant Jacob is also behind us.’" For he said, "I will calm his anger with the gift going ahead of me. Afterward I will see his face; perhaps he will receive me favorably."
The gift went on ahead of him, while he spent that night in the camp.
He got up during the night, took his two wives, his two servant women, and his eleven sons, and brought them across to the wilderness of Jabbok.
He took them and brought them across the stream, and he brought across everything he had.
Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until dawn broke.
When the man saw that he could not overpower him, he touched his hip socket, and Jacob’s hip socket was dislocated as he wrestled with him.
He said to him, "Let me go, for dawn has broken." But Jacob said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
He said to him, "What is your name?" And he said, "Jacob."
He said to him, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, because you have held your own against an angel and against a man and have prevailed.”
Jacob asked him, "Tell me your name." He said to him, "Why do you ask about my name?" And he blessed him there.
Jacob named that place Penuel, "For I have seen an angel face to face, and my life has been spared."
The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip socket.
For this reason, to this day the Israelites do not eat the sciatic nerve at the socket of the thigh, because he touched the socket of Jacob’s thigh at the sciatic nerve.
Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming with four hundred men. He divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two servant women.
He put the servant women and their children first, Leah and her children behind them, and Rachel and Joseph last.
He himself went ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him, and they wept.
Esau looked up and saw the women and children. He said, “Where did you get these?” He answered, “They are the children God has given your servant.”
The servant women and their children came forward and bowed down.
Leah and her children also approached and bowed down. Afterward, Rachel and Joseph also approached and bowed down.
Esau said, “What do you mean by this whole company that met me?” Jacob answered him, “It was so that I might find favor in my lord’s eyes.”
Esau said to him, “I have enough for myself. My brother, [?] what is yours.”
Jacob said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, accept my gift from my hands, because now I have seen your face as one sees the face of an angel, and you have welcomed me.”
“Accept my blessing that I have brought you, because God has been merciful to me and because I have everything.” He urged him, and he accepted it.
Esau said to him, “Let us set out and go, and I will go alongside you.”
Jacob said to him, “My lord knows that the children are young, and that the sheep and cattle nursing their young are in my care. If I drive them hard for even one day, the whole flock will die.”
“Let my lord go ahead of his servant, and I will travel gently, at the pace of the livestock ahead of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
Esau said to him, “Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me.” Jacob said, “Why should I need that? Let me find favor in my lord’s eyes.”
That day Esau returned on his way to Seir.
Jacob traveled to Succoth and built himself a house, and he made shelters for his livestock. That is why he named that place Succoth.
Jacob came to Shalem, a town of Shechem in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan-aram, and he camped opposite the town.
He bought a piece of the field from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred ewes, and pitched his tent there.
He set up an altar there and called it El, the God of Israel.
Dinah, Leah’s daughter whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to see the women of the land.
Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the ruler of the land, saw her. He took her, slept with her, and violated her.
His heart went out to Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. He loved the young woman and [?] to the young woman’s heart.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, “Get me this young woman as a wife.”
Jacob heard that they had defiled his daughter Dinah. His sons were with the livestock in the field, and Jacob kept silent until they came.
Hamor, Shechem’s father, went out to Jacob to speak with him.

Jacob’s sons came from the field. When they heard, the men were grieved and very angry, because they had committed an act of defilement in Israel and violated Jacob’s daughter. Such a thing must not be done.
Hamor spoke with them and said to them, “My son Shechem’s heart desires your daughter. Give her to him as a wife.”
“Intermarry with us. Give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves.”
“Live with us. The land is here before you. Settle in it, trade in it, and acquire property in it.”
Shechem said to her father and her brothers, “Let me find favor in your eyes, and I will give whatever you tell me.”
Ask me for a very large bride-price and gifts, and I will give whatever you tell me. Just give me this young woman as my wife.
Jacob’s sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, because they had defiled their sister Dinah.
They said, “We cannot do this—give our sister to an uncircumcised man—because that would be a disgrace to us.
But we will agree to you on this condition: that you become like us and circumcise every male, just as we are circumcised.
Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves. We will live with you and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, we will take our daughter and leave.”
Their words pleased Hamor and his son Shechem.
The young man did not delay in doing this, because he desired Jacob’s daughter. He was more honored than anyone else in his father’s household.
Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of their town and spoke to the men of their town, saying,
“These men are at peace with us. Let them live in the land and trade in it. Look, the land has ample room for them. Let us take their daughters as our wives and give them our daughters.
But the men will agree to live with us and become one people only on this condition: that we circumcise every male, just as they are circumcised.
Their wealth, their possessions, and all their livestock will be ours. Only let us agree to their terms, and they will live with us.”
All who went out through the gate of his town listened to Shechem and his father Hamor. They circumcised every male, all who went out through the gate of his town.
On the third day, when their pain was severe, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, each took his sword. They entered the town quietly and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, took Dinah from Shechem’s house, and left.
Jacob’s sons came upon the slain and plundered the town because they had defiled their sister Dinah.
They took their sheep, cattle, and donkeys, both those in the town and those in the fields.
They carried off all their possessions and took all their dependents and their wives captive. They plundered everything in the town.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought trouble on me by making me hated among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I am few in number. They will gather against me and attack me, and I will be destroyed, both I and my household.”
They said, “Should our sister be treated like a prostitute?”
The Lord said to Jacob, “Get up, go up to Bethel, and settle there. Make an altar there to God, who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother Esau.”
Jacob said to the members of his household and everyone with him, “Remove the foreign gods that are among you. Purify yourselves and change your clothes.
Come, let us go up to Bethel. There I will make an altar to God, who answered me in the day of my distress and was with me on the journey I made.”
They gave Jacob all the foreign gods they had and the earrings in their ears. Jacob buried them under the terebinth tree near Shechem.
They set out, and the fear of God fell on the towns around them, so they did not pursue Jacob and his sons.
Jacob came to Luz in the land of Canaan—that is, Bethel—he and all the people with him.
He built an altar there and called that place Bethel, because God had appeared to him there when he was fleeing from his brother Esau.
Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried below Bethel, under the terebinth tree. He named it the Terebinth of Weeping.
God appeared to Jacob again when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him.
God said to him, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but your name will be Israel.” And he named him Israel.
God said to him, “I am El Shaddai, God. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation and an assembly of nations will come from you, and kings will come from your own body.”
“The land that I promised on oath to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give the land to your descendants after you.”
God went up from him at the place where he had spoken with him.
Jacob set up a pillar at the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured a drink offering on it and poured oil on it.
Jacob named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
He set out from Bethel and traveled on, with about a parasang of land still to cross before reaching Ephrath. Rachel gave birth, and her labor was difficult.
When her labor became difficult, the midwife said to her, “Do not be afraid, for this too is a son for you.”
As her life was departing and she was dying, she named him Son of My Sorrow, but his father named him Benjamin.
Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over Rachel’s grave. It is the pillar of Rachel’s grave to this day.
Israel moved on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Geder.
While Israel was living in that land, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard about it. Jacob had twelve sons.
The sons of Leah were Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, were Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, were Gad and Asher. These were Jacob’s sons who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, the city of giants, which is Hebron in the land of Canaan, where Abraham and Isaac had lived.
Isaac lived one hundred and eighty years.
Isaac became ill and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him in the tomb that his father Abraham had bought.
These are the descendants of Esau. Esau is Edom.
Esau took his wives from the women of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon the Hivite,
and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau, and Basemath bore Reuel.
Oholibamah gave birth to Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah. These were the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, everyone in his household, all his livestock, and all the possessions he had acquired in the land of Canaan, and went to the land of Seir, away from his brother Jacob.
For their possessions were too great for them to live together, and the land where they lived could not support them because of their livestock.
Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
These are the descendants of Esau, the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau’s sons: Reuel, the son of Basemath, Esau’s wife; and Eliphaz, the son of Adah, Esau’s wife.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s son, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. These were the sons of Adah, Esau’s wife.
These were the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These were the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
These were the sons of Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon, and the wife of Esau. She bore Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah to Esau.
These were the chiefs among Esau’s sons. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, were Chief Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Zepho, and Chief Kenaz.
Chief Gatam, Chief Korah, and Chief Amalek. These were the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom. These were the sons of Adah.

These were the sons of Reuel, Esau’s son: Chief Nahath, Chief Zerah, Chief Shammah, and Chief Mizzah. These were the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom. These were the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
These were the sons of Oholibamah, Esau’s wife: Chief Jeush, Chief Jaalam, and Chief Korah. These were the sons of Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah and the wife of Esau.
These were Esau’s sons, and these were their chiefs. Esau is Edom.
These were the sons of Seir, the Horites who lived in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah.
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These were the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Homam. Lotan’s sister was Timna.
These were the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Awim.
These were the sons of Zibeon: Ana and Anah. This was the Anah who found water in the wilderness while tending the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
These were the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah.
These were the sons of Dishon: Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
These were the sons of Ezer: Kelhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
These were the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
These were the chiefs of the Horites: Chief Lotan, Chief Shobal, Chief Zibeon, and Chief Anah.
Chief Dishon, Chief Ezer, and Chief Dishan. These were the chiefs of the Horites, according to their chieftaincies in the land of Seir.
These were the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites.
Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom, and the name of his town was Dinhabah.
Bela died, and Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah reigned in his place.
Jobab died, and Husham from the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
Husham died, and Hadad son of Bedad, who killed the Midianites in the fields of Moab, reigned in his place. The name of his town was Avith.
Hadad died, and Samlah from Masrekah reigned in his place.
Samlah died, and Shaul from Rehoboth on the River reigned in his place.
Shaul died, and Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.
Baal-hanan son of Achbor [?] died, and Hadad became king after him. The name of his city was Pau, and the name of his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, son of Me-zahab.
These are the names of Esau’s chiefs, according to their clans and their generations, by their names: Chief Timna, Chief Alvah, and Chief Jetheth;
Chief Oholibamah, Chief Elah, and Chief Pinon;
Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, and Chief Mibzar;
Chief Magdiel and Chief Iram. These were the chiefs of the Edomites according to their dwelling places in the land they possessed. This was Esau, the father of the Edomites.
Jacob lived in the land where his father had lived, in the land of Canaan.

This is the family history of Jacob. Joseph was seventeen years old and was tending the flock with his brothers. He was growing up with the sons of Zilpah and the sons of Bilhah, his father’s wives. Joseph brought their father a bad report about them.
Israel loved Joseph more than all his other sons because he was a son born to him in his old age, and he made him a multicolored robe.
His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all of them, and they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.
Joseph had a dream and told it to his brothers, and they hated him even more.
He said to them, “Listen to this dream I had.
There we were, binding sheaves in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright. Then your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to my sheaf.”
His brothers said to him, “Are you really going to reign over us? Are you really going to rule over us?” They hated him still more because of his dreams and his words.
He had another dream and told it to his brothers. He said to them, “Look, I have had another dream: the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”

He told his father and his brothers, and his father rebuked him and said to him, “What is this dream you have had? Will I and your mother and your brothers really come and bow down to the ground before you?”
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
Joseph’s brothers went to pasture their father’s flock at Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, “Your brothers are tending the flock in Shechem. Come, let me send you to them.” He answered him, “Here I am.”
His father said to him, “Go and see whether your brothers and the flock are well, and bring me back word.” Jacob sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering in the field. The man asked him, “What are you looking for?”
He said, “I am looking for my brothers. Tell me where they are tending the flock.”
The man said to him, “They have moved on from here. I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” Joseph went after his brothers and found them in Dothan.
They saw him from a distance, and before he came near them, they were plotting to kill him.
They said to one another, “Here comes that dreamer!
Come, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. We will say that a wild animal ate him, and we will see what becomes of his dreams.”
Reuben heard this and rescued him from their hands. He said to them, “Let us not take his life.”
Reuben said to them, “Do not shed blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him.” This was so that he could rescue him from their hands and return him to his father.
When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of the multicolored tunic he was wearing.
They took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.
They sat down to eat bread. They looked up and saw a caravan of Arabs coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying aromatic gum, balm, and terebinth nuts, which they were taking down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, “What will we gain by killing our brother and covering up his blood?
Come, let us sell him to the Arabs and not lay our hands on him, because he is our brother, our own flesh.” His brothers listened to him.
Midianite merchants passed by, and they pulled Joseph up out of the pit. They sold Joseph to the Arabs for twenty pieces of silver, and they brought him to Egypt.
Reuben returned to the pit, and Joseph was not there. He tore his clothes.
He returned to his brothers and said to them, “Where is the boy? And where am I to go?”
They took Joseph’s tunic, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the tunic in its blood.
They sent the multicolored tunic and had it brought to their father. They said, “We found this. Examine the tunic and see whether it is your son’s or not.”
He recognized it and said, “It is my son’s tunic. A wild animal has eaten him. My son Joseph has surely been torn to pieces.”
Jacob tore his clothes, tied sackcloth around his waist, and mourned his son for many days.
All his sons and all his daughters came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, “I will go down to Sheol mourning my son.” His father wept for him.
The Midianites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and chief executioner.
At that time Judah went down away from his brothers and turned aside to a man, an Adullamite [?], named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man. Her name was Shua. He married her and slept with her.
She became pregnant and bore him a son, and he named him Er.
She conceived again and gave birth to a son, and he named him Onan.
She again bore a son, and he named him Shelah. She stopped bearing children when she had given birth to him.
Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn. Her name was Tamar.
Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord put him to death.
Judah said to his son Onan, “Sleep with your brother’s wife and fulfill your duty as her brother-in-law, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. Whenever he had intercourse with his brother’s wife, he spilled his semen on the ground so that he would not provide offspring for his brother.
What he did was evil in the sight of the Lord, and he put him to death as well.

Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he said, “Otherwise he too may die like his brothers.” So Tamar went and lived in her father’s house.
Much time passed, and Judah’s wife, the daughter of Shua, died. After Judah was comforted, he went up to his sheep shearers at Timnah, together with his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
Tamar was told, “Look, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”

She took off her widow’s clothes, covered herself with a veil, adorned herself, and sat at the crossroads on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah had grown up, but she had not been given to him in marriage.
Judah saw her and thought she was a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
He turned aside to her by the road and said to her, “Come, let me sleep with you,” for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said to him, “What will you give me to sleep with me?”
He said, “I will send a young goat from the flock.” She said, “If you give me a pledge until you send it.”
He said, “What pledge shall I give you?” She said, “Your signet ring, your shawl, and the staff in your hand.” He gave them to her and slept with her, and she became pregnant by him.
She got up and left, took off her veil, and put on her widow’s clothes.
Judah sent the young goat through his friend the Adullamite to retrieve the pledge from the woman, but he did not find her.
He asked the men of the place, “Where is the prostitute who sits at the crossroads?” They said, “There is no prostitute here.”
He returned to Judah and said, “I did not find her. The men of the place also say, ‘There is no prostitute here.’”
Judah said, “Let her keep it, so that I do not become a laughingstock. Look, I sent this young goat, but you did not find her.”
After three months, Judah was told, “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has acted as a prostitute, and now she is pregnant through prostitution.” Judah said, “Bring her out and let her be burned.”
As they were bringing her out, she sent word to her father-in-law: “I am pregnant by the man who owns these things.” She said, “Identify whose signet ring, shawl, and staff these are.”
Judah recognized them and said, “She is more righteous than I am, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.” He did not sleep with her again.
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twins in her womb.
While she was giving birth, one put out his hand. The midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it around his hand, saying, “This one will come out first.”
When he drew back his hand, his brother came out, and she said, “What a breach you have made for yourself!” So she named him Perez.
Afterward his brother came out, with the scarlet thread on his hand, and she named him Zerah.
The Midianites brought Joseph down to Egypt. Potiphar, an Egyptian who was Pharaoh’s eunuch and chief executioner, bought him from the Arabs who had brought him down there.
The Lord was with Joseph, and he became a successful man in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that the Lord was with him and that the Lord made everything he did succeed.
Joseph found favor in his sight and served him. He put him in charge of his household and entrusted everything he owned to him.

From the time he put him in charge of his household and everything he owned, the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s household because of Joseph. The Lord’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in the house and in the field.
He left everything he had in Joseph’s hands and did not concern himself with anything in Joseph’s care except the food he ate. Joseph was handsome in form and attractive in appearance.
After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph and said to him, “Sleep with me.”
But he refused and said to his master’s wife, “Look, with me here, my master does not concern himself with what is in his house. He has entrusted everything he owns to me.
No one in this house is greater than I am. He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How could I do this great evil and sin against God?”
Although she spoke to him every day, he would not listen to her and would not sleep beside her or be with her.
One day Joseph went into the house to do his work, and none of the household servants were there in the house.
She caught him by his garment and said to him, “Sleep with me.” But he left his garment in her hands and fled outside.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hands and fled outside,
she called the members of her household and said to them, “Look! He has brought us a Hebrew slave to mock us. He came in to sleep with me, but I cried out loudly.
When he heard me raise my voice and cry out, he left his garment beside me and fled outside.”
She kept his garment beside her until his master came into the house.
She told him the same story: “The Hebrew slave you brought us came in to mock me.”
“When I raised my voice and shouted, he left his garment in my hands and fled outside.”
When his master heard his wife’s words, as she told him, “This is what your slave did to me,” his anger flared.
His master took him and put him in prison, where the king’s prisoners were confined. So he remained there in prison.
The Lord was with Joseph and showed him kindness, granting him favor in the sight of the prison warden.
The prison warden entrusted all the prisoners in the prison to Joseph, and Joseph was responsible for everything done there.
The prison warden did not check on anything entrusted to Joseph, because the Lord was with him, and the Lord made everything he did succeed.
After these things, the chief cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the chief baker offended their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh became angry with his two eunuchs, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
He put them in prison, in the house of the captain of the guard, where Joseph was imprisoned.
The captain of the guard put Joseph in charge of them, and he attended to them. They remained in prison for some time.
Both of them had dreams on the same night, each his own dream, each dream with its own interpretation—the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were confined in prison.
Joseph came to them in the morning and saw that they were troubled.
He asked Pharaoh’s officials, who were with him in custody in his master’s house, “Why do your faces look so sad today?”
They said to him, “We have had dreams, but there is no one to interpret them.” Joseph said to them, “Interpretations belong to God. Tell me your dreams.”
The chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream and said to him, “In my dream, there was a vine in front of me.
On the vine were three branches. As it budded, its leaves sprouted, and its clusters ripened into grapes.
Pharaoh’s cup was in my hands. I took the grapes and squeezed them into Pharaoh’s cup, and I placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hands.”
Joseph said to him, “This is the interpretation of your dream: the three branches are three days.
After three days, Pharaoh will remember you and restore you to your position. You will place the cup in Pharaoh’s hand, as you used to do when you served him as cupbearer.
But remember me when things go well for you. Show me kindness and faithfulness, mention me to Pharaoh, and get me out of this prison.
For I was indeed stolen from the land of the Hebrews, and here too I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this pit.”
The chief baker saw that Joseph had given a favorable interpretation, and he said to Joseph, “In my dream too, there were three baskets of white bread on my head.
In the top basket were all kinds of food for Pharaoh, made by a baker, and the birds were eating them from the basket above my head.”
Joseph answered him, “This is the interpretation of your dream: the three baskets are three days.
After three days, Pharaoh will take your head off you and hang you on a tree, and the birds will eat your flesh off you.”
On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, Pharaoh held a feast for all his servants. He remembered the chief cupbearer and the chief baker among his servants.
He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hands.
But he hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had interpreted their dreams for them.
The chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph; he forgot him.
After two years, Pharaoh had a dream: he was standing by the river.
Seven cows came up out of the river, fine-looking and fat, and grazed in the meadow.
Then seven other cows came up out of the river after them, ugly and thin, and stood beside the other cows on the riverbank.
The ugly, thin cows ate the seven fine-looking, fat cows. Then Pharaoh woke up.
He fell asleep and dreamed a second time. There were seven heads of grain growing on one stalk, full and good.
And there were seven heads of grain, thin and scorched by the hot wind, sprouting after them.
The thin heads of grain swallowed the seven plump, full heads. Then Pharaoh woke up and realized it was a dream.
In the morning Pharaoh was troubled in spirit. He sent for all the magicians and all the wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them for Pharaoh.
Then the chief cupbearer spoke before Pharaoh and said, “Today I remember my offenses.
Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put us in prison in the house of the captain of the guard—me and the chief baker.
He and I dreamed dreams on the same night, each of us having a dream with its own meaning.
A young Hebrew man was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him, and he interpreted our dreams for us, giving each man the interpretation of his dream.
Things happened to us just as he had interpreted: Pharaoh restored me to my position, but hanged the other man.”
Then Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they hurried him out of the dungeon. He shaved, changed his clothes, and came before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have had a dream, and there is no one to interpret it. But I have heard about you, that you can hear a dream and interpret it.”
Joseph answered Pharaoh, “Do you think that without God I can give Pharaoh a favorable answer?”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “In my dream, I was standing on the bank of the river.
Seven cows came up out of the river, fat and fine-looking, and grazed in the meadow.
And look, seven other cows came up after them, scrawny, ugly, and very thin. I had never seen cows as bad as these in all the land of Egypt.
The thin, ugly cows ate the first seven fat cows.
It went inside them, but no one could tell that it had gone inside them. They looked as bad as before. Then I woke up.
Again I saw in my dream seven heads of grain growing on one stalk, full and good.
And there were seven heads of grain, thin and scorched by the hot wind, sprouting after them.
The thin heads of grain swallowed the seven good heads. I told the magicians, but no one could explain it to me.”
Joseph said to Pharaoh, “Pharaoh’s dream is one and the same. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. It is one and the same dream.
The seven weak, ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven thin heads of grain scorched by the hot wind will be seven years of famine.
This is what I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
Seven years are coming, with great abundance throughout the land of Egypt.
After them, seven years of famine will arise. All the abundance that there was throughout the land of Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will devastate the land.
The abundance in the land will no longer be recognizable because of the famine that follows, for it will be very severe.
The dream was repeated to Pharaoh twice because the matter has been firmly decided by God, and God is hurrying to bring it about.
Now let Pharaoh find a wise and discerning man and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh proceed and appoint officials over the land of Egypt, and let them collect a fifth of the produce in the land of Egypt during the seven years of abundance.
Let them gather all the grain of these good years that are coming and store grain under Pharaoh’s authority. Let them keep the grain in the towns.
The grain will be kept in reserve for the land during the seven years of famine that will come throughout the land of Egypt, so that the land will not perish in the famine.
The proposal pleased Pharaoh and his servants.
Pharaoh said to his servants, “Can a man like this be found, one who has the Spirit of God in him?”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has made all this known to you, there is no one as wise and discerning as you.
You will be in charge of my household, and all my people will be governed by your word. Only in regard to the throne will I be greater than you.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Look, I have put you in authority over the whole land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph’s hand. He dressed him in fine linen clothes and placed a gold necklace around his neck.
He seated him in his second chariot, and they called out before him, “Father and ruler!” He gave him authority over all the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I, Pharaoh, have commanded that without your permission no one may lift a hand or a foot throughout the land of Egypt.”

Pharaoh named Joseph Zaphenath-paneah, meaning “one to whom hidden things are revealed.” He gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, as his wife. Joseph went out over the whole land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Joseph left Pharaoh’s presence and traveled throughout the land of Egypt.
During the seven years of abundance, the land accumulated produce in storehouses.
He stored all the grain of the seven years of abundance that occurred in the land of Egypt, putting the grain in the towns. In each town he stored the grain from its fields and the surrounding area.
Joseph stored grain like the sand of the sea, in such great quantities that he grew tired of counting it, for it was beyond counting.
Two sons were born to Joseph before the year of famine came. Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore them to him.
Joseph named his firstborn son Manasseh, “because God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s household.”
He named the other Ephraim, “because God has made me fruitful in the land of my bondage.”
The seven years of abundance in the land of Egypt came to an end.
The seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all the lands, and there was no bread throughout the land of Egypt.
The whole land of Egypt was hungry, and the people pleaded with Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.”
The famine spread over the whole land. Joseph opened the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians. The famine grew severe in the land of Egypt.
People from the whole earth came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine had grown severe throughout the land of Egypt.
Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt, and Jacob said to his sons, “Do not be afraid.”
Look, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us from there, so that we may live and not die.
Ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, with his brothers, because he said, “Some harm might happen to him.”
The sons of Israel came to buy grain among the others who were going, because the famine had become severe in the land of Canaan.
Joseph was the ruler over the land, and he sold grain to all the people of the land. Joseph’s brothers came and bowed down to him with their faces to the ground.

Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, but he acted deceptively toward them and spoke harshly to them. He said to them, “Where are you from?” They said, “We have come from the land of Canaan to buy grain.”
Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them, and he said to them, “You are spies! You have come to see the condition of the land.”
They said, “No, our lord! Your servants have come to buy grain.”
“We are all sons of one man. We are honest men, and your servants have never been spies.”
Joseph said to them, “No, that is not so! You have come to see the condition of the land.”
They said to him, “We, your servants, are twelve brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father today, and one is no more.”
Joseph said to them, “It is just as I told you: you are spies.”
“This is how you will be tested. No! By Pharaoh’s life, you will not leave here unless your youngest brother comes here.”
“Send one of you to bring your brother, while you remain imprisoned. Your words will be tested to see whether you have spoken truthfully. Otherwise, by Pharaoh’s life, you are indeed spies!”
He put them in prison for three days.
On the third day Joseph said to them, “Do this and live, for I fear God.”
“If you are honest men, let one of your brothers remain confined in the prison where you have been held. The rest of you go and take grain to the hungry people in your households.”
“Bring your youngest brother to me, so that your words may be believed and you will not die.” And they did so.
They said to one another, “We are truly guilty concerning our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we did not listen to him. That is why this distress has come upon us.”
Reuben answered them, “Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy? But you did not listen. Now his blood is being demanded of us as well.”
They did not know that Joseph understood, because an interpreter stood between them.
He turned away from them and wept. Then he returned to them and spoke with them. He took Simeon from among them and bound him before their eyes.
Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, to return each man’s money to his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. This was done for them.
They loaded their grain onto their donkeys and left there.
At the lodging place, one of them opened his sack to give his donkey fodder, and he saw his money lying at the opening of his sack.

He said to his brothers, “My money has been returned! Here it is at the opening of my sack!” Their hearts trembled, and they looked at one another in dismay, saying, “What is this that God has done to us?”
They came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan and told him everything that had happened to them. They said to him:
“The man who is lord of the land spoke harshly to us and considered us spies in the land.
We said to him, ‘We are honest men, and we are not spies.
We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no more, and the youngest is with our father today in the land of Canaan.’
The man who is lord of the land said to us, ‘This is how I will know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, take grain for the hungry people in your households, and go.
Bring your youngest brother to me. Then I will know that you are not spies but honest men. I will give your brother back to you, and you may trade in the land.’”
As they were emptying their sacks, there was each man’s bundle of money at the opening of his pack. When they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, “You have bereaved me! Joseph is no more, and Simeon is no more, and you would take Benjamin away. All this has fallen on me!”
Reuben said to his father, “You may kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Entrust him to me, and I will return him to you.”

But he said, “My son will not go down with you, because his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother’s children. If an accident happens to him on the journey you are taking, you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow.”
The famine grew severe in the land.
When they had finished eating the grain they had brought from Egypt, their father Jacob said to them, “Go down and buy us a little grain.”
Judah said to him, “The man solemnly warned us, saying, ‘You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.’
If you send our brother with us, we will go down and buy grain for ourselves.
But if you do not send him, we will not go down, because the man said to us, ‘You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.’”
Their father Israel said to them, “Why did you bring this trouble on me by telling the man that you had a brother?”

They said, “The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our family, asking, ‘Is your father still alive? Do you have a brother?’ We told him in response to these questions. How could we have known that he would say, ‘Bring your brother down’?”
Judah said to his father Israel, “Send the boy with us, and let us get up and go, so that we may live and not die—we, you, and our households.
I will stand as surety for him; you may hold me responsible for him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, I will bear the guilt before my father for all my days.
If we had not delayed, we could already have returned twice by now.”

Their father Israel said to them, “If that is how it is, do this: take some of the best produce of the land in your containers, and bring the man a gift—a little balm and a little honey, resin and ladanum, pistachios and almonds.
Take twice the money with you, and take back the money that was returned in the openings of your packs. Perhaps it was a mistake.
“Take your brother, get up, and return to the man.”
May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, so that he sends your other brother and Benjamin back with you. As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.”
The men took this gift and twice the money, and they took Benjamin with them. They set out and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph.
Joseph saw Benjamin with them and said to the steward of his house, “Bring the men into the house, slaughter an animal, and prepare it, because the men will eat with me at noon.”
The servant did as Joseph had said and brought the men into Joseph’s house.

They were afraid when they were brought into Joseph’s house. They said, “We are being brought in because of the money that was returned in our packs the first time, so that they can overpower us and plot against us, making us slaves and taking our donkeys.”
They approached the man in charge of Joseph’s household and spoke with him at the entrance to the house.
They said to him, “Please, our lord, we came down the first time to buy grain.
When we reached the lodging place, we opened our sacks, and there was each man’s money in the mouth of his sack. We have brought our money back with us, its full weight.
We have also brought other money with us to buy grain. We do not know who put our money in the mouths of our sacks.”
He said to them, “Peace to you. Do not be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your money.” Then he brought Simeon out to them.
The servant brought the men into Joseph’s house. He gave them water, and they washed their feet. He also gave their animals fodder.
They prepared the gift for Joseph’s arrival at noon, because they had heard that they would eat there.
Joseph came into the house, and they brought him the gift they had with them into the house and bowed down to the ground before him.
He asked how they were and said to them, “Is your father well, the old man you told me about? Is he still alive?”
They said, “Your servant our father is well.” They told him, “He is still alive.” Then they knelt and bowed down.
He looked up and saw Benjamin, his brother, his mother’s son, and said to them, “Is this your youngest brother, whom you told me about?” Then he said, “May God have mercy on you, my son.”
Joseph hurried away because his feelings for his brother welled up and he wanted to weep. He went into his room and wept there.
Then he washed his face and came out. He controlled himself and ordered that food be served to them.
They served him separately, them separately, and the Egyptians who ate with him separately, because the Egyptians could not eat with the Hebrews, since that was defilement to the Egyptians.
They reclined before him, the oldest according to his seniority and the youngest according to his youth. The men looked at one another in astonishment.
They received portions from his table, and Benjamin’s portion was five times larger than the portions of all the others. They drank and became drunk with him.
He commanded the man in charge of his household, saying, “Fill the men’s sacks with as much grain as they can carry, and put each man’s money in the mouth of his sack.
Take my silver cup and put it in the mouth of the youngest one’s sack, along with the money for his grain.” The servant did as Joseph had said.
When morning came, the men were sent on their way with their donkeys.
They had left the city but had not gone far when Joseph said to the man in charge of his household, “Get up, pursue the men, and catch up with them. Say to them, ‘Why have you repaid good with evil?
This is the cup my master drinks from, and he also uses it for divination. You have done wrong in what you have done.’”
He caught up with them and spoke these words to them.
They said to him, “Our lord must not say such things! Far be it from your servants to do such a thing!
Look, we brought back from the land of Canaan the money we found in the mouths of our sacks. How could we steal gold or silver from your master’s house?
Whichever of your servants it is found with shall die, and we too will become slaves to our lord.”
He said to them, “Even now, let it be as you have said: the one it is found with will become my slave, but you will be free of blame.”
They hurried and each lowered his sack to the ground, and each opened his sack.
They searched, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest. The cup was found in Benjamin’s load.
They tore their clothes. Each man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city.
Judah and his brothers went in to Joseph, who was still there, and fell to the ground before him.
Joseph said to them, “What is this you have done? Don’t you know that a man like me can certainly practice divination?”
