Judah said, “What can we say to my lord? What can we tell him? How can we prove our innocence? Your servants’ sin has been discovered before God. Here we are, my lord’s slaves, both we and the one in whose possession the cup was found.”
He said to them, “Far be it from me to do this! The man with whom the cup was found will be my slave. But you may go up in peace to your father.”
Judah approached him and said, “I beg you, my lord, let your servant speak a word before you, my lord. Do not let your anger flare up against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh.
My lord asked his servants, ‘Do you have a father or a brother?’
We said to my lord, ‘We have an elderly father and a young son born to him in his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother’s children. His father loves him.’
You said to your servants, ‘Bring him down to me so that I may set my eyes on him.’
We said to my lord, ‘The boy cannot leave his father. If he leaves his father, he will die.’
You said to your servants, ‘Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you will not see my face again.’
When we went up to your servant our father, we told him what my lord had said.
Your servant our father said to us, ‘Go back and buy us a little grain.’
We said to our father, ‘We cannot go down. If our youngest brother goes down with us, we will go down, because we cannot see the man’s face unless our youngest brother is with us.’
“Your servant, our father, said to us, ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons.’”
“‘One went away from me, and I said, “He has certainly been killed.” I have not seen him to this day.’”
‘If you take this one away from me too, and harm comes to him, you will bring me down in my old age to Sheol in misery.’
Now, when we go to your servant our father and the boy is not with us—his life is as dear to him as his own—
when he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die. Your servants will bring your servant our father down in his old age to Sheol in sorrow.
“For your servant pledged himself to our father as guarantor for the boy, saying, ‘If I do not bring him back to you, I will bear the guilt before my father all my life.’”
Now let your servant remain as my lord’s slave in place of the boy, and let the boy go up with his brothers.
For how can I go up to my father if the boy is not with me? I could not bear to see the misery that would befall my father.”
Joseph could no longer restrain himself before all those standing in his presence. He said, “Send everyone away from me.” No one remained with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers.
He wept aloud, and the Egyptians heard him, and it was heard in Pharaoh’s household.
Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph, your brother. Is my father still alive?” His brothers could not answer him, because they were afraid in his presence.
Joseph said to his brothers, “Come closer to me.” They came closer to him, and he said to them, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold to the Egyptians.
Now do not be distressed or upset that you sold me here, for God sent me ahead of you to provide sustenance.
For the famine has been in the land for two years now, and there are still five years in which there will be neither sowing nor reaping.
God sent me ahead of you to preserve a remnant for you and to keep you alive through a great deliverance in the land.
So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, master over his entire household, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
Hurry and go up to my father and tell him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me master over all Egypt. Come down to me without delay.
Settle in the land of Goshen, and you will be near me—you, your children, the members of your household, your flocks, your cattle, and everything you have.
I will provide for you there, because the famine will continue for another five years, so that you, your household, and everything you have do not perish.’
Your own eyes and the eyes of my brother Benjamin can see that it is my own mouth speaking to you.
Tell my father about all the honor I have in Egypt and everything you have seen. Hurry and bring my father down here.
He threw his arms around his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.
He kissed all his brothers and wept over them. After that, his brothers spoke with him.
The news was heard in Pharaoh’s household: ‘Joseph’s brothers have come.’ Pharaoh and his servants were pleased with the news.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, ‘Tell your brothers, “Do this: load your animals with grain and go carry it to the land of Canaan.
Bring your father and the members of your households and come to me. I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you will eat the richest produce of the land.”
You have authority. Tell your brothers, “Do this: take wagons from the land of Egypt for your wives and your families, and bring your father and come.”’
“Do not be concerned about leaving your belongings, because the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.”
The sons of Israel did so. Joseph gave them wagons at Pharaoh’s command, and he gave them provisions for the journey.
To all of them, to each man, he gave a set of clothes. To Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five sets of clothes.
To his father he sent the following: ten male donkeys loaded with the best things of the land of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, wine, and provisions for his father’s journey.
He sent them off, and they went. He told them, ‘Do not quarrel on the way.’
They went up from Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, to their father Jacob.
They told him, ‘Joseph is still alive! He is ruler over all the land of Egypt.’ His heart was stunned, because he did not believe them.
They told him everything Joseph had said to them. Jacob saw the wagons Joseph had sent to carry him, and the spirit of their father Jacob was refreshed.
He said, ‘It is a great thing for me that my son Joseph is still alive. I will go and see him before I die.’
Israel set out with everything he had and came to Beersheba. He offered a sacrifice to the God of his father Isaac.
God spoke to Israel in a vision at night, saying, ‘Jacob, Jacob!’ He answered, ‘Here I am.’
He said to him, ‘I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, because I will make you into a great nation there.
I will go down with you, and I will bring you up again. Joseph will lay his hands on your eyes.’
Jacob left Beersheba. The sons of Israel carried their father Jacob, their families, and their wives in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
They took their livestock and the possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan and came to Egypt—Jacob and all his descendants with him.
His sons and grandsons were with him, his daughters and granddaughters; he brought all his descendants with him to Egypt.
These are the names of the children of Israel who entered Egypt, Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn.
The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman.
The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Job, and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are the sons of Leah whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, along with his daughter Dinah. His sons and daughters numbered thirty-three people in all.
The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arod, and Areli.
The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.
These are the children of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah. She bore these to Jacob—sixteen people.
The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin.
Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph in the land of Egypt. Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore them to him.
The sons of Benjamin were Bela, Acbar [?], Ashkel [?], Gera, Naaman, Ahi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These are the children of Rachel whom she bore to Jacob—fourteen people.
The sons of Dan: Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These are the children of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel. She bore these to Jacob—seven people in all.
All the people who entered Egypt with Jacob, who were his own offspring, apart from the wives of Jacob’s sons, numbered sixty-six people in all.
The sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt numbered two people. All the people of Jacob’s household who entered Egypt numbered seventy.
He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph, to appear before him in Goshen. Then he came to the land of Goshen.
Joseph had his chariots made ready and went up to Goshen to meet his father Israel. He appeared before him, threw his arms around his neck, and wept on his neck again.
Israel said to Joseph, “Now I can die, after seeing your face, my son, since you are still alive.”
Joseph said to his brothers and his father’s household, “I will go up and tell Pharaoh and say to him, ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
The men are shepherds, for they are livestock owners. They have brought their flocks, their cattle, and everything they have.’”
When Pharaoh calls you and asks you, ‘What is your occupation?’

Tell him, ‘Your servants have been livestock keepers from their youth until now, both we and our fathers,’ so that you may settle in the land of Goshen, because all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.

Joseph came and informed Pharaoh, saying to him, ‘My father and my brothers, with their flocks, their cattle, and everything they own, have come from the land of Canaan. They are now staying in the land of Goshen.’
He took five men from among his brothers and presented them before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked Joseph’s brothers, ‘What is your occupation?’ They said to Pharaoh, ‘Your servants are shepherds, both we and our fathers, from our youth.’

They said to Pharaoh, ‘We have come to live in the land because there is no pasture for your servants’ flocks, since the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. Now let your servants settle in the land of Goshen.’
Pharaoh said to Joseph, ‘Your father and your brothers have come to you.

The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best part of the land. Let them settle in the land of Goshen. If you know that there are capable men among them, put them in charge of all the livestock I own.’
Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked Jacob, ‘How many are the years of your life?’

Jacob said to Pharaoh, ‘The years of my life as a foreign resident are one hundred and thirty years. The years of my life have been few and troubled, and they have not reached the years my fathers lived during their time as foreign residents.’
Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and Jacob went out from Pharaoh’s presence.
Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best part of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.
Joseph supplied his father, his brothers, and his father’s entire household with grain according to the size of each family.
There was no grain anywhere in the land, because the famine was very severe. The whole land of Egypt and the land of Canaan were devastated by the famine.
Joseph collected all the money found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan in payment for the grain they were buying. Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh’s house.

When the money in the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan was exhausted, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said to him, ‘Give us grain so that we do not die before you, for the money has run out.’
Joseph said to them, ‘Give me your livestock, and I will give you grain in exchange for your livestock, if the money has run out.’
They brought him their livestock, and Joseph gave them grain in exchange for horses, flocks, cattle, and donkeys. That year he supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock.

That year ended, and they came to him the following year and said to him, ‘We will not hide from our lord that all the money is gone and that our livestock belongs to our lord. Nothing remains before our lord except ourselves and our lands.

Why should we perish before your eyes, both we and our lands? Buy us and our lands in exchange for food, and we and our lands will be Pharaoh’s servants. Give us seed so that we may live and not die, and so that the land will not become desolate.’
Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, because the Egyptians each sold their fields, since the famine had become severe upon them. So the land became Pharaoh’s.
As for the people, he moved them from town to town, from one end of Egypt’s territory to the other.
Only the priests’ land he did not buy, because the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh. They lived on the allowances Pharaoh gave them; therefore they did not sell their land.
Joseph said to the people, ‘Today I have bought you and your lands for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you to sow in the land.

When the harvest comes in, you are to give one-fifth to Pharaoh. The other four shares will be yours for seed for the fields, for your food, for food for your households, and for food for your dependents.’
They said, ‘You have saved our lives. May we find favor in our lord’s eyes, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.’
Joseph established this as a law concerning the land of Egypt, lasting to this day: one-fifth belongs to Pharaoh. Only the priests’ land did not become Pharaoh’s.
Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. They grew strong there, increased, and became very numerous.
Jacob lived in the land of Egypt for seventeen years. The days of Jacob, the years of his life, amounted to 147 years.

When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand under my loins, and I will make you swear by the Lord. Show me kindness and faithfulness, and do not bury me in Egypt.”
“When I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their tomb.” Joseph said, “I will do as you say.”
He said, “Swear to me.” So he swore to him, and Israel bowed down over the top of his staff.
After these things, Joseph was told, “Your father is ill.” He took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, with him.
They told Jacob, “Look, your son Joseph has come to you.” Israel gathered his strength and sat up on the bed.
Israel said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me.
He said to me, ‘Look, I will bless you and make you numerous. I will make you a company of peoples, and I will give this land to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession.’
Now your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in the land of Egypt are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine; they will be like Reuben and Simeon to me.
The children you father after them will be yours. They will be called by their brothers’ names in receiving their inheritance.

As for me, when I was coming from Paddan-aram, Rachel died, to my sorrow, in the land of Canaan along the way, about a parasang’s journey before reaching Ephrath. I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.”
Israel saw Joseph’s sons and said to him, “Who are these?”
Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” He said, “Bring them to me, and I will bless them.”
Israel’s eyes had grown dim with age, and he could not see well. Joseph brought them near him, and he kissed them and embraced them.
Israel said to Joseph, “I did not expect to see your face, but now God has shown me your descendants as well.”
He brought them out from before his knees, and they bowed before him with their faces to the ground.
Joseph took both his sons, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right, and brought them near him.
Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head. He crossed his hands, for Manasseh was the firstborn.
Jacob blessed his son Joseph and said, “The God whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac pleased, the God who has sustained me from my youth until this day,

the angel who has rescued me from every evil—may he bless the boys. May my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac be carried on through them, and may they increase and become numerous in the land.”
Joseph saw that his father had laid his right hand on Ephraim’s head, and he was displeased. He took hold of his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head and place it on Manasseh’s head.
Joseph said to his father, “Not like this, my father! This one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”

But his father refused and said, “I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, and he too will become great. But his younger brother will become greater than he, and his descendants will become a multitude of nations.”
He blessed them that day and said, “Through you Israel will be blessed, and they will say, ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” He placed Ephraim before Manasseh.
Israel said to Joseph, “Look, I am dying, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers.
I have given you one portion more than your brothers, which I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow.”
Jacob called his sons and said to them, “Gather together, and I will tell you what will happen to you in the days to come.”
Gather and listen, sons of Jacob. Listen to Israel your father.
Reuben, you are my firstborn, my strength and the beginning of my vigor, surpassing in dignity and surpassing in power.
You went astray like water; you will not excel, because you went up to your father's bed. Indeed, you defiled my bed and went up.
Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of anger are part of their nature.
My soul did not enter their council, and my honor did not descend into their assembly, because in their anger they killed men, and in their fury they tore down a wall.
Cursed is their anger, because it is fierce, and their fury, because it is cruel. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies. Your father's sons will bow down to you.
Judah is a lion's cub. You have come up from the killing, my son. He crouched and lay down like a lion, like a lion's cub. Who will rouse him?
The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until the one to whom it belongs comes. The nations will wait expectantly for him.
He will tie his young donkey to the vine, his donkey's colt to the vine branch. He will wash his clothing in wine and his covering in the blood of grapes.
His eyes are bloodshot from wine, and his teeth are white from milk.
Zebulun will dwell on the seashores. He will be at a harbor for ships, and his boundary will extend to Sidon.
Issachar is a mighty man, lying down between the paths.
He saw that his dwelling place was pleasant and his land was good. He bent his shoulder to servitude and became subject to tribute.
Dan will judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a snake on the road, a viper on the paths, biting the horse's heel and throwing its rider backward.
I have waited for your salvation, LORD.
Gad will go out with a troop, and he will bring up the rear.
Asher's land is good, and he will provide food for kings.
Naphtali is a swift messenger, delivering beautiful words.
Joseph is a flourishing son, a flourishing son watered by a spring, a sturdy structure that rises along the wall.
They fought with him and increased in number, and the commanders of troops hated him.
His bow turned back in strength, and his arms were scattered through the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob and through the name of the shepherd of the stone of Israel.
May your father's God help you, and may God Almighty bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lies below, and blessings of breasts and wombs.
Your father's blessings have surpassed the blessings of my parents, reaching to the hope of the everlasting hills. May they rest on Joseph's head, on the head of the crowned one among his brothers.
Benjamin is a ravenous wolf. In the morning he will eat the plunder, and in the evening he will divide what he has carried off.
All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what Jacob their father said to them. He spoke to them and blessed them, blessing each one according to his own blessing.
Their father gave them instructions and said to them, “I am being gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
in the double cave in the field opposite Mamre, in the land of Canaan—the field Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial property.
There they buried Abraham and his wife Sarah. There they buried Isaac and his wife Rebekah, and there I buried Leah.
The field and the cave in it were purchased from the descendants of Heth.”
When Jacob finished giving instructions to his sons, he stretched out his feet on the bed, became ill, and died. He was gathered to his people.
Joseph fell upon his father’s face, wept over him, and kissed him.
Joseph ordered his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father, and the physicians embalmed Israel.
Forty days were completed for him, for that is how long the embalming takes. The Egyptians mourned him for seventy days.
When the days of mourning for him had passed, Joseph said to Pharaoh’s household, “If I have found favor in your eyes, speak to Pharaoh and say,
‘My father made me swear an oath, saying to me, “Look, I am dying. Bury me in the tomb I bought for myself in the land of Canaan.” Now let me go up and bury my father, and I will return.’”
Pharaoh said, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.”
Joseph went up to bury his father. All Pharaoh’s servants went up with him, along with the elders of his household and all the elders of the land of Egypt.
Joseph’s entire household, his brothers, and his father’s household went up with him. They left only their dependents, their flocks, and their cattle in the land of Goshen.
Chariots and horsemen also went up with him, and it was a very large company.
They came to the threshing floors of Atar, beyond the Jordan, and there they made a great and intense lamentation. Joseph observed seven days of mourning for his father.

When the Canaanite inhabitants of the land saw the mourning at the threshing floors of Atar, they said, “This is a great mourning for the Egyptians.” That is why they named the place Abel-mizraim, which is beyond the Jordan.
His sons did for him just as he had instructed them.
They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the double cave in the field that Abraham had bought as a burial property from Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre.
After burying his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and everyone who had gone up with him to bury his father.
When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they were afraid and said, “Perhaps Joseph will hold a grudge against us and repay us for all the evil we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father gave this instruction before his death:

‘Say this to Joseph: Please forgive your brothers’ wrongdoing and their sins, for they did evil to you.’ Now forgive the wrongdoing of the servants of your father’s God.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before him, saying, “Here we are, your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Do not be afraid, for I am under God.”
You intended evil against me, but God intended it for good, to bring about what has happened today and keep many people alive.
Now do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your households.” He comforted them and spoke reassuringly to them.
Joseph lived in Egypt, he and all his father’s household. Joseph lived 110 years.
Joseph saw Ephraim’s descendants to the third generation. The children of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were also born on Joseph’s knees.
Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely remember you and bring you up from this land to the land he swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”
Joseph made the Israelites swear an oath, saying, “God will surely remember you. Bring my bones up from here with you.”
Joseph died at the age of 110. They embalmed him and placed him in a coffin in Egypt.
